clue.text: Sight of glasses not quite full

indicators.note: not quite full means the word loses its final letter, stopping just short of complete

parts.note: glasses worn on the nose are spectacles

explanation.surface: Someone describes their eyewear as a pair of half-empty glasses, perhaps of drink.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Glasses' tempts as drinking glasses not quite full; it is eyewear, SPECTACLES, and 'not quite full' drops its last S.
explanation.definitionFit: A spectacle is a striking sight or show put on for viewers.

clue.text: Put forward pawn to open

parts.note: P is the chess abbreviation for a pawn
to lead is to open play, as in leading the first card

explanation.surface: A chess player advances a pawn to start the game.
explanation.walkthrough: The chess picture makes 'Put forward' look like moving a piece; it is the definition, as in putting forward an argument.
explanation.definitionFit: To plead a case is to argue or urge it, putting it forward before others.

clue.text: Here, you risk an offence in company

indicators.note: in places the offence inside the company's abbreviation

parts.note: an offence is a sin, with the article kept

explanation.surface: A warning that committing a crime while employed by a firm is dangerous.
explanation.definitionFit: A gambling house is the place where people stake money on chance.

clue.text: Broad Street, said to be a meeting place

parts.note: a venue is a place where people meet or an event is held

explanation.surface: A wide road is described as a spot where people gather.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Said to be' joins definition and wordplay: the broad street, spoken, is just 'a venue'.
explanation.definitionFit: An avenue is a wide street, often lined with trees.

clue.text: Like the poetry of Cyril in translation?

indicators.note: in translation suggests the name is turned into another form, so its letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: Someone asks whether a poet named Cyril's verse reads better translated.
explanation.definitionFit: Lyric verse expresses personal feeling and was originally sung, an adjective for that kind of poem.

clue.text: Histrionic quality? Lyric hate it at break!

indicators.note: break tells the solver to smash the preceding words apart and rebuild them

explanation.surface: An overdramatic outburst: a singer declares they hate a lyric and must take a break.
explanation.definitionFit: Being histrionic means being showily dramatic, as an actor on stage might be.

clue.text: One from France went along with solo

parts.note: un is French for one
to accompany is to go along with someone

explanation.surface: A Frenchman tagged along with a lone performer.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Solo' reads as a person but is an adjective, the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: A solo performance is one done alone, without others playing along.

clue.text: For example, Leicester's trial for fleecing

parts.note: the Leicester is a breed of sheep, so this is a sheep's
a hearing is a trial in court

explanation.surface: A court case in the city of Leicester concerns somebody conning people.
explanation.walkthrough: Leicester looks like the English city; here it is a breed of sheep. 'Fleecing' pretends to mean swindling.
explanation.definitionFit: Shearing removes a sheep's wool, its fleece, so fleecing is a playful synonym.

clue.text: Accountant ineffectual without motivation?

parts.note: CA is a chartered accountant
something ineffectual is useless

explanation.surface: A hopeless accountant who simply cannot be bothered.
explanation.definitionFit: Something with no reason or cause behind it is groundless, lacking any motive.

clue.text: In this branch of mathematics, position the circle to touch lines

parts.note: to set is to place or position
O is shaped like a circle
RY is short for railway, a set of lines

explanation.surface: Geometry instructions: place a circle so it is tangent to some lines.
explanation.walkthrough: 'To touch' only links the pieces; the geometry vocabulary disguises them.
explanation.definitionFit: The study of collections of objects and their membership is a foundational mathematical field.

clue.text: Trophy of battle in our times?

indicators.note: in puts the conflict inside the era's abbreviation

parts.note: AD, anno Domini, marks the years of the present era
a war is a large-scale battle

explanation.surface: A medal won for fighting in a modern conflict.
explanation.definitionFit: A prize or trophy is something given in recognition of achievement.

clue.text: Reserve of ready money, we are told

indicators.note: we are told signals a word heard spoken rather than seen written

parts.note: ready money is cash in hand

explanation.surface: A rumour that someone has a stockpile of available funds.
explanation.definitionFit: A cache is a hidden store or stockpile kept for later use.

clue.text: Broken English in Hull, say?

indicators.note: in places the abbreviation inside the ship's space

parts.note: the hold is the hull or cargo space of a ship

explanation.surface: Poor English is spoken in the Yorkshire city of Hull.
explanation.walkthrough: Hull looks like the English city; with 'say' it is an example of a ship's HOLD. 'Broken' is the definition, not describing the English.
explanation.definitionFit: A hull that is holed has been pierced, so damaged or broken.

clue.text: Colour not used by Titian, when nature provides it

indicators.note: provides it says the phrase itself supplies the letters, tucked across its two words

explanation.surface: Titian's auburn hair needed no dye because nature gave it that colour.
explanation.walkthrough: Titian red is an auburn shade; the reddish dye is what a natural redhead does not need.
explanation.definitionFit: Henna is a reddish-brown dye from a plant, used on hair, so a shade a natural redhead never needs.

clue.text: Dance in prison?

definitions.meaning: a West Indian dance of bending backwards under a bar
old slang for a jail or confinement

explanation.definitionFit: The limbo is a Caribbean dance under a lowered bar; in old slang it also meant jail, so being in limbo was being locked up.

clue.text: Nightclub inventor? Not half!

indicators.note: Not half means only half the word is kept, the rest dropped

parts.note: a discoverer finds or invents something new

explanation.surface: Someone asks whether a club's founder was clever and gets an emphatic yes.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Not half!' is British slang for 'definitely'; here it removes the back half of DISCOVERER.
explanation.definitionFit: A disco is a club where people dance to recorded music at night.

clue.text: Remove outer skin of pickle

definitions.meaning: to strip off a surface layer by rubbing

explanation.definitionFit: To scrape is to strip off a surface layer; a scrape is also a fix or predicament, as is a pickle.

clue.text: Take in meaning

explanation.definitionFit: To import is to bring goods in from abroad; import is also significance or sense.

clue.text: Underwriters of unusual means

indicators.note: unusual signals the word is put into an odd, rearranged order

explanation.surface: Insurers who are unusually wealthy.
explanation.walkthrough: At Lloyd's of London, the insurance market, the individual backers who underwrite risks are called Names.
explanation.definitionFit: The members of Lloyd's who underwrite insurance with their own money are known by this title.

clue.text: It may grow on walls of church, in changing line

indicators.note: in puts the church abbreviation inside the rearranged word
changing tells the solver to alter the order of the word's letters

explanation.surface: Something growing on a church's walls in a shifting row.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Changing' makes LIEN, which 'in' wraps round the church abbreviation. 'Walls of church' looks like one phrase, but 'of' is only a link.
explanation.definitionFit: A lichen is a slow-growing organism that spreads over stone and bark.

clue.text: Pair liberal in car…

indicators.note: in puts the party abbreviation inside the car

parts.note: a coupé is a two-door car

explanation.surface: Two politicians from the Liberal party sharing a car.
explanation.definitionFit: Two things or people together make a pair.

clue.text: … and in abundance at disco

explanation.definitionFit: Borrowed from French, the phrase means aplenty; it is also the name for a discotheque or nightclub.

clue.text: Almost lose sight of evil sprite

indicators.note: Almost means the phrase stops one letter short of its end

parts.note: to lose one's sight is to go blind

explanation.surface: A malevolent fairy nearly fades from view.
explanation.definitionFit: A goblin is a mischievous or wicked creature of folklore.

clue.text: He is up in Argentina with a nasty cough

indicators.note: nasty suggests the words are mangled into a new order

explanation.surface: A man laid up in Argentina with a bad cold.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Up' pretends to mean bedridden; it means up on horseback, as a South American cowboy is.
explanation.definitionFit: The South American cowboy rides the pampas of Argentina on horseback.

clue.text: People at the bar in jockeys' colours

definitions.meaning: senior barristers, who wear silk gowns
racing shirts in an owner's colours

explanation.definitionFit: Senior barristers (Queen's or King's Counsel) wear silk gowns and are called this; jockeys' racing shirts in owners' colours are too.

clue.text: Riddle of Lear's craft?

definitions.meaning: a coarse strainer for soil or gravel
the boat in Edward Lear's nonsense poem The Jumblies

explanation.definitionFit: A riddle is a coarse strainer; in Edward Lear's poem The Jumblies they went to sea in one.

clue.text: Theme of a singer

explanation.definitionFit: A tenor is the general drift of a text; it is also a high male voice or its singer.

clue.text: Suspicion of footprint

definitions.meaning: a mark or track left behind

explanation.definitionFit: A trace is a slight hint or suggestion; it is also a mark or track left behind.

clue.text: Possibly, he pre-selects a runner at Aintree

indicators.note: Possibly hints that a different arrangement of the following letters is wanted

explanation.surface: A racing tipster picks a horse for the meeting at Aintree.
explanation.walkthrough: Aintree, near Liverpool, hosts the Grand National, the famous jumps race over fences.
explanation.definitionFit: A horse that races over fences and ditches runs at the Grand National course.

clue.text: Tall, thin people training runners

definitions.meaning: supporting runner beans as they climb

explanation.definitionFit: Lanky people are called this; the canes also support climbing runner beans in a garden.
